title: Enum Classes in C++ and Their Advantage over Enum DataType - GeeksforGeeks
content:
An enumeration (enum) is a user-defined data type that consists of a fixed set of named integral constants. Each enumerator is automatically assigned an integer value starting from 0, unless a different value is explicitly specified.

  • Declared using the enum keyword.
  • Represents a fixed set of named integer constants.
  • Improves code readability by replacing integer literals with meaningful names.

Example: The following program demonstrates declaring and using a traditional enum.

C++ 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
enum roll_no {
    satya = 70,
    aakanskah = 73,
    sanket = 31,
    aniket = 05,
    avinash = 68,
    shreya = 47,
    nikita = 69,
};
int main()
{
    enum roll_no obj;
    obj = avinash;
    cout << "The roll no  of avinash=" << obj;
}

Output
The roll no  of avinash=68

Explanation

  • roll_no is an enumeration containing named constants.
  • Each enumerator represents an integer value.
  • The variable obj stores one of the enumerator values and is printed as its corresponding integer.

Syntax

// Declaration
enum class EnumName { Value1, Value2, Value3 };

// Initialization
EnumName obj = EnumName::Value1;

Limitations of Traditional Enums

Although traditional enums improve code readability, they have several limitations. These limitations were addressed with the introduction of enum classes in C++11.

Enumerator Name Conflicts 

Enumerators declared in a traditional enum are placed in the surrounding scope. As a result, different enums cannot contain enumerators with the same name.

  • Enumerator names are not scoped.
  • Name collisions occur when multiple enums contain identical enumerators.
  • Results in a compilation error.

Example: The following program demonstrates a name conflict between two traditional enums.

CPP 
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    // Defining enum1 Gender
    enum Gender { Male,
                  Female };

    // Defining enum2 Gender2 with same values
    // This will throw error
    enum Gender2 { Male,
                   Female };

    // Creating Gender type variable
    Gender gender = Male;
    Gender2 gender2 = Female;

    cout << gender << endl
         << gender2;

    return 0;
}

Output

error: 'Male' conflicts with a previous declaration

Explanation: Both Gender and Gender2 declare the enumerators Male and Female. Since traditional enums place their enumerators in the same scope, the compiler reports a redeclaration error.

Enumerator and Variable Name Conflicts

Since enumerators exist in the surrounding scope, a variable cannot have the same name as an enumerator.

  • Enumerator names occupy the enclosing scope.
  • Variables cannot reuse an enumerator name.
  • Causes a compilation error.

Example: The following program demonstrates a name conflict between an enumerator and a variable.

CPP 
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    // Defining enum1 Gender
    enum Gender { Male,
                  Female };

    // Creating Gender type variable
    Gender gender = Male;

    // creating a variable Male
    // this will throw error
    int Male = 10;

    cout << gender << endl;

    return 0;
}

Output

error: 'int Male' redeclared as different kind of entity

Explanation: The enumerator Male already exists in the current scope. Declaring another variable with the same name causes a redeclaration error.

Lack of Type Safety 

Traditional enums are not strongly typed. Different enumeration types can be compared because they are implicitly converted to integers.

  • Different enums can be compared unintentionally.
  • Enumerators are implicitly converted to integer values.
  • May lead to unexpected program behavior.

Example: The following program demonstrates the lack of type safety in traditional enums.

CPP 
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    // Defining enum1 Gender
    enum Gender { Male,
                  Female };

    // Defining enum2 Color
    enum Color { Red,
                 Green };

    // Creating Gender type variable
    Gender gender = Male;
    Color color = Red;

    // Upon comparing gender and color
    // it will return true as both have value 0
    // which should not be the case actually
    if (gender == color)
        cout << "Equal";

    return 0;
}

Output 

warning: comparison between 'enum main()::Gender'

Explanation: Gender::Male and Color::Red both have the integer value 0. During comparison, they are implicitly converted to integers, making the comparison valid even though the two enums represent unrelated concepts.

Enum Classes  (Modern C++ Solution)

Enum classes solve the issues of traditional enums by making them strongly typed and scoped.

  • Provides strong type safety and scoped enumerators.
  • Prevents implicit conversions and naming conflicts.

Enum classes solve the issues of traditional enums by making them strongly typed and scoped.

Example: The following program demonstrates the use of enum classes.

CPP 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main()
{

    enum class Color { Red,
                       Green,
                       Blue };
    enum class Color2 { Red,
                        Black,
                        White };
    enum class People { Good,
                        Bad };

    // An enum value can now be used
    // to create variables
    int Green = 10;

    // Instantiating the Enum Class
    Color x = Color::Green;

    // Comparison now is completely type-safe
    if (x == Color::Red)
        cout << "It's Red\n";
    else
        cout << "It's not Red\n";

    People p = People::Good;

    if (p == People::Bad)
        cout << "Bad people\n";
    else
        cout << "Good people\n";

    // gives an error
    // if(x == p)
    // cout<<"red is equal to good";

    // won't work as there is no
    // implicit conversion to int
    // cout<< x;

    cout << int(x);

    return 0;
}

Output
It's not Red
Good people
1

Explanation

  • Enum classes have separate scopes, so names don’t conflict.
  • Only same enum class values can be compared; no implicit int conversion.
  • Different enum classes cannot be directly compared, and casting is needed to print integer values.

Specifying the Underlying Type

By default, the underlying type of an enum class is int. However, C++ allows specifying a different integral type such as char, short, or unsigned int. This is useful when memory optimization is required.

  • The underlying type is specified using a colon (:).
  • Any integral type can be used as the underlying type.
  • Reduces memory usage when a smaller type is sufficient.

Syntax

enum class EnumName : UnderlyingType {

Value1,

Value2,

...

}

Example: The following program compares the size of a traditional enum and an enum class with a custom underlying type.

C++ 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
enum rainbow{
    violet,
    indigo,
    blue,
    green,yellow,orange,red
}colors;
enum class eyecolor:char{
    blue,green,brown
}eye;
int main() {

    cout<<"size of enum rainbow variable: "<<sizeof(colors)<<endl;
    cout<<"size of enum class eyecolor variable:"<<sizeof(eye)<<endl;
    return 0;
}

Output
size of enum rainbow variable: 4
size of enum class eyecolor variable:1

Explanation

  • rainbow is a traditional enum and uses the default underlying type (int), so its size is 4 bytes.
  • eyecolor specifies char as its underlying type, reducing its size to 1 byte.
  • Choosing an appropriate underlying type can help optimize memory usage.

Advantages of Enum Classes

Enum classes provide several advantages over traditional enums.

  • Strong type safety prevents unintended comparisons.
  • Enumerators remain scoped within their enum class.
  • Prevents implicit conversion to integers.
  • Allows specifying the underlying integral type.
  • Produces cleaner and more maintainable code.

Traditional Enum Vs Enum Class

FeatureTraditional EnumEnum Class
ScopeEnumerators are placed in the surrounding scopeEnumerators are scoped inside the enum class
Type SafetyNot strongly typedStrongly typed
Implicit ConversionAutomatically converts to intNo implicit conversion
Enumerator Name ConflictsPossiblePrevented
Underlying TypeUses int by defaultCustom underlying type can be specified
